title: Galileo, Einstein, and the unexpected origins of relativity
subtitle: Cracking the problem of relative motion
author: Sebastián Murgueitio Ramírez
introduction: One of Galileo Galilei’s many contributions to science was his understanding of relative motion – that the physics within a system do not depend on the speed at which the system moves relative to external systems, provided the original system is not accelerating. This idea would go on to form the foundations for Einstein’s Relativity Principle which required that the physics of the system does not depend on the inertial frame chosen to study it. Though subtly different, modern physics often conflates these ideas leading to conflicting resolutions to Galileo’s initial problem. Sebastián Murgueitio Ramírez argues that by distinguishing between an "internal" and "external" version of the principle, we can right this, clarify its original meaning and appreciate just how far ahead of his time Galileo truly was.
body:
When going about our daily routine, it is too easy to forget that we are moving around the Sun at thousands of kilometers per hour. It certainly does not seem as if we were moving that fast when we walk around the neighborhood or when we look at the night sky. In fact, that things do not seem as if we are moving that fast (or moving at all) was for more than a thousand years cited as a reason in favor of a geocentric universe, with the Earth motionless at its centre. But given that we are moving fast around the Sun, why, then, do we not notice such motion?

Almost 400 years ago, in Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems, Galileo provides an answer to that question. In “Day Two” of that book, Galileo presents the following now very famous passage with the aim of illustrating that the motion of the Earth, just as the uniform motion of a ship, is not detectable from “within”:

Shut yourself up with some friend in the main cabin below decks on some large ship, and have with you there some flies, butterflies, and other small flying animals. Have a large bowl of water with some fish in it; hang up a bottle that empties drop by drop into a wide vessel beneath it. With the ship standing still, observe carefully how the little animals fly with equal speed to all sides of the cabin. The fish swim indifferently in all directions; the drops fall into the vessel beneath; […] When you have observed all these things carefully […], have the ship proceed with any speed you like, so long as the motion is uniform and not fluctuating this way and that. You will discover not the least change in all the effects named, nor could you tell from any of them whether the ship was moving or standing still. In throwing something to your companion, you will need no more force to get it to him whether he is in the direction of the bow or the stern, with yourself situated opposite. […] the butterflies and flies will continue their flights indifferently toward every side, nor will it ever happen that they are concentrated toward the stern, as if tired out from keeping up with the course of the ship, from which they will have been separated during long intervals by keeping themselves in the air. […] the cause of all these correspondences of effects is the fact that the ship's motion is common to all the things contained in it, and to the air also (Galilei, 1967, p. 186).

Galileo’s important insight is that just as a person in the cabin would not be able to tell that the ship is moving uniformly by looking at the various objects around them (water drops, fish, butterflies, and so on), we also are not able to tell that the Earth is moving around the Sun simply by looking at our surroundings. This is true, of course, but why?

The first key lies in the last sentence of the passage, where Galileo says that such motion is undetectable because everything in the cabin, including the observer and the air, are moving together.  In other words, here Galileo is hinting at the fact that motion is relative; the observer is moving relative to the shore and to the ocean, but not to the cabin, and this explains, according to Galileo, why everything inside the cabin looks the same to the observer regardless of whether the ship is moving or not. Although Copernicus in the XVI century and even Buridan already in the XIV century alluded to early versions of this idea (Browne, 2020 p. 207-213), Galileo seems to have been the first one offering a systematic exposition, not just in the fragment cited above but throughout much of “Day Two” of his book.

The second key lies in the notion of uniform motion. In the passage, Galileo says that “so long as the motion is uniform”, the passenger will not notice the ship’s motion. But what, exactly, is uniform motion?

We learn in school that it corresponds to motion in a straight line with constant speed. In fact, this is the kind of motion that a body subject to no forces has, a discovery also attributed to Galileo in what is often called “the law of inertia”, which later became Descartes’ first law, and then, Newton’s first law. As it turns out, inertial motion is not really the same in Galileo and Newton.  For Newton, inertial motion is motion with constant speed along a straight line, whereas for Galileo, it consists of circular motion with constant speed. For instance, a ball moving in a hypothetical frictionless surface around the globe would be moving inertially according to Galileo, but not according to Newton and Descartes (although they would not use this exact terminology). Thankfully, this difference does not matter in the case of the ship, for the arc that the ship traces relative to the centre of the Earth in a matter of hours is so small that it is well approximated by a straight line.

Let’s agree, then, that for practical purposes, the ship is moving inertially in both Galileo’s and Newton’s sense. How can this be used to explain that things inside of it look the same regardless of its motion? Put differently, how is the uniformity of the motion related to the relativity of motion noted by Galileo?

Perhaps the key to answering these questions resides in applying the law of inertia not only to the ship, but also to the objects inside of it. According to this law, an object at rest in the cabin subject to no forces will remain at rest, and one that is in motion in the cabin will remain in motion, provided, of course, that the ship itself is moving inertially. Thus, one might think that objects preserving their inertial motion is all that is really required to make sense of what is happening inside the ship, and in fact, one might think that this is ultimately what is behind’s Galileo’s own reasoning. Unfortunately, things are not so simple. Most of the objects Galileo describes, including the fish and the butterflies, are examples of objects that are subject to forces, and so are objects not moving inertially. Thus, we need to go beyond the law of inertia to make sense of the behavior of objects inside the cabin!

Let’s grant, then, that we cannot simply appeal to the law of inertia to explain why all the objects inside the ship’s cabin behave as they do as the ship moves uniformly. But perhaps there is an indirect sense in which this law can help. Notice that since the ship is moving uniformly, it can be used to define an inertial frame. Imagine, in particular, that we “attach” a coordinate system to the ship’s cabin. Using this inertial frame, we can then define the motions of the bodies inside the ship’s cabin, regardless of whether they are moving inertially or accelerating. Once we have this inertial frame, we can then appeal to what is known as the Relativity Principle, that says, roughly, that the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames (this principle was discussed by Poincaré in 1904, but became well-known thanks to Einstein, who used it in his era-making 1905 paper on special relativity).

In particular, we can propose the following explanation: given the Relativity Principle, both the inertial frame “attached” to the shore when the ship is at rest in the port, and the one attached to the ship when the latter is moving uniformly must agree as to what the laws of all physical systems in the ship are. More specifically, if one frame “says” that an object in the cabin obeys law L, then the other frame must say the same thing. Since the laws of objects in the ship are the same in the moving (ship) frame and the rest (shore) frame, it is expected that the behavior of objects in the ship’s cabin is independent of whether the ship is moving or not.

We thus seem to have finally “solved” Galileo’s ship using principles of modern physics! Not so quickly! The problem is that we have not properly distinguished two similar but different situations.

In one, we study a certain physical system, say a water drop inside the cabin as it is seen simultaneously from the perspective of a person in the shore as the ship moves in front of them and by a person inside the cabin moving together with the ship. In the second situation, we study two copies of the same physical system, say two identical water drops, one as seen from the perspective of a person in the ship when the ship is at rest, and the other one as seen from the perspective of the same person when the ship (and the person in it) is moving uniformly.

Although these two definitions are related, it is important to emphasize that they are different.

It should be clear that this second situation is the one that is relevant to explaining Galileo’s ship, as the relevant observer is one moving together with the ship. What is not so clear is which of the two situations in question is the Relativity Principle supposed to apply to, and so whether that principle can even help us understand Galileo’s ship.

As I have shown in a recent paper, it turns out that these two situations are often conflated in the physical and philosophical literature on the Relativity Principle. To be concrete, sometimes physicists say that according to this principle, the laws of a given physical system must be the same as seen from the perspective of two (or more) inertial frames, even though the motion of that system is different in the different frames due to the relativity of motion, as illustrated by the first situation mentioned above.  On other occasions, they say that according to this principle, the laws of a physical system as seen in a given frame are the same as the laws of a boosted version of that system as seen in a boosted frame, as happens in the second situation (here “boosted” simply means that the velocity of the system or frame is higher or lower compared to the original system or frame). I call the first kind of definition of the Relativity Principle “external”, for it concerns a single system as seen by two external observers, and the second one “internal”, as it concerns a system as seeing by an observer co-moving with it (like the observer inside the ship).  Although these two definitions are related, it is important to emphasize that they are different.

In fact, I have recently argued that certain simple physical systems, such as classical waves or ideal springs, are compatible with the internal definition of the Relativity Principle, but not with the external one.

For example, imagine that inside the ship someone is playing the guitar. For the person in the ship, the classical wave equation captures how the strings vibrate. Crucially, the equation works in all inertial frames co-moving with the guitar regardless of what the ship’s velocity relative to the shore is, which is precisely what we expect from the internal version of the Relativity Principle. On the other hand, one could easily check that if the ship is moving passed the shore, one cannot use the classical wave equation to model the vibrations of that string as seen from a frame at rest in the shore, even though that same equation does work well in a frame co-moving with the ship. The issue is that the differential equation itself, which captures the law associated with the vibrations, is different in the cabin and in the shore (this is not true of the differential equations used to model a ball in free fall in the cabin, nor of the wave equations for electromagnetic waves when we consider different inertial frames related to one other by Lorentz boosts). So, it is simply not true that the laws for a given system are always the same in every inertial frame, even if it is true that such laws are always the same in any inertial frame that is co-moving with the system. Thus, the internal version of the Relativity Principle seems to be much more general than the external one. This is good for our purposes given that it is the internal version the one that really matters to Galileo’s ship, since we only care about how things inside the cabin look to a person moving together with the ship.

Distinguishing the external and the internal versions of the Relativity Principle helps us avoid confusion when teaching classical mechanics and special relativity. For example, when teaching classical mechanics, it is common to say things like “the laws of classical systems are invariant under Galilean transformations” and “all inertial frames are equivalent.”  But notice that these phrases are ambiguous; one can either mean that the laws of physical systems are the same in all inertial frames that are co-moving with the system, as the internal version of the Relativity Principle requires, or one can mean that the laws are the same in all inertial frames regardless of whether they are co-moving with the system or not, as the external version requires. If one means the former, that is certainly true, but if one means the latter, then there will be some counterexamples such as the ones given by classical waves.

The internal version of the Relativity Principle is important but cannot be enough in our explanation. For although it is in fact crucial that the laws of the objects in the cabin remain the same even after one boosts these objects, one also needs to guarantee that the motion in the cabin as seen by the observer is preserved.

Similarly, when teaching Special Relativity, one says things like “the laws of physical systems are invariant under Lorentz transformations” and “all inertial frames are equivalent.” Again, these phrases are ambiguous and might pick up an external or internal version of the relativity principle. Interestingly, in the case of electromagnetic waves, it is the external version of the principle the one which is particularly interesting, and the one that was important to Einstein when developing the theory of Special Relativity! After all, not only the speed of a single light beam is the same as seen in all frames, but the wave equation itself is able to capture that beam in all frames, as Einstein famously showed in his 1905 paper.

The internal version of the Relativity Principle is important but cannot be enough in our explanation. For although it is in fact crucial that the laws of the objects in the cabin remain the same even after one boosts these objects, one also needs to guarantee that the motion in the cabin as seen by the observer is preserved. After all, as the external version of the Relativity Principle makes it clear, preserving the laws is not sufficient for preserving the motions; a single drop as seen by two observers in two frames will have different motions, but will satisfy the same laws.

At the end of the day, one cannot help but appeal to the fact that by boosting together the system and the observer, one guarantees that the relative motion between them is preserved, as Galileo had suggested when saying that “the ship's motion is common to all the things contained in it, and to the air also”. So Galileo was close to the right answer from the beginning, prior to even the development of classical mechanics! But the apparent simplicity of Galileo’s answer is misleading, and one does need modern physics, and in particular the internal version of the Relativity Principle, to really appreciate why. For if the laws of physical systems had depended on the velocity of the systems, as many believed was indeed the case for some systems in the 19th century due to a possible ether, then the relative motion between systems and observers might have been disrupted by boosts, in which case, pace Galileo, the butterflies and flies might not have continued their flights indifferently toward every side of the cabin.
